title: SQL and Data Modeling Interview Pack
description: Practice relational modeling, SQL queries and PostgreSQL performance with small synthetic examples.

questions.question: How would you model enrollment when each student can take several courses and each course can have several students?
paraphrases: Design a relational schema for students and courses without duplicate enrollments.
answerOutline: Put students and courses in separate tables with their own primary keys.
Reference both from an enrollment table and make their pair unique.
Store properties of an enrollment, such as the enrollment date, in that table.
Model a course offering or term separately if a student can repeat a course.

questions.question: A report must list every course with a count of active enrollments, including zero. Why did adding a WHERE filter on enrollment status remove some courses?
paraphrases: How do you count matching children while keeping parents that have no match?
answerOutline: A left join fills unmatched enrollment columns with NULL.
Filtering by enrollment status in WHERE drops those rows.
Move the status predicate into the join or count conditionally while keeping the left join.
Count a non-null enrollment column when the join filter is used so the placeholder row contributes zero.

questions.question: How would you return exactly one most recent enrollment per student when two enrollments can share a timestamp?
paraphrases: What makes a latest-row-per-group query deterministic when the ordering column ties?
answerOutline: Partition rows by student, ordering by enrollment time descending.
Add a stable unique tie-breaker and explain what it means for tied rows.
Use ROW_NUMBER and select row one in an outer query.
Account for missing timestamps explicitly if the column permits NULL.

questions.question: Two transactions each see one seat left in a course and insert an enrollment. How would you preserve the seat limit?
paraphrases: How would you prevent concurrent bookings from exceeding a capacity constraint?
answerOutline: A count followed by an insert can race when both transactions see the same available seat.
One design locks the shared course row before reading availability and inserting in the same transaction.
Another uses serializable transactions and retries the entire transaction on a serialization failure.
Require all enrollment paths to use the same rule and test with overlapping transactions.

questions.question: A PostgreSQL report reads most rows in a large table. Why might a sequential scan be cheaper even when its filter column is indexed?
paraphrases: Why might PostgreSQL choose a sequential scan for a query with a usable index?
answerOutline: An index lookup can still require fetching table rows.
For many matches, reading the table in order can cost less than scattered lookups.
Compare estimated and actual row counts on representative data.
Consider cache state, selectivity, and whether an index-only scan can supply all needed columns.
